title: What drives the emergence of symbolic mechanisms in large language models?
claim: A model solves abstract rule tasks by abstracting symbols from context, then rotating query tokens in role subspaces to gate the output.
layout: Single panel, bottom-to-top and left-to-right flow, colored boxes with curved arrows
description: A single diagram showing how the model processes an ABB task, read from the bottom up. At the bottom are input tokens: an in-context example (tok13, tok49, tok49) and a query (tok6, tok17), each marked by a brace. Above the in-context tokens is a green box labeled 'Symbol abstraction heads'. It tags the tokens A, B, B, and a dashed arrow links the repeated tok49 tokens. A curved arrow carries the abstracted symbol 'B' to a blue box labeled 'Subspace rotation'. The query tokens are labeled tok6 (A) and tok17 (B), and they feed into that box. Two circular arrows inside it show the rotation. Above the box, the labels swap and the output is tok17. Black arrows show the flow, and the left and right labels name the stages.
caption: Illustration of Symbolic Mechanisms Learned by Model. Problems consist of an in-context example governed by either an ABA or ABB (pictured) rule constructed with arbitrary tokens, followed by an incomplete query example that must be completed according to the same rule. Symbol abstraction heads process the in-context example, identifying the symbol (A or B) associated with the third token. Query tokens are copied into role-specific (A vs. B) subspaces of the residual stream at the final position, and a rule-dependent (ABA vs. ABB) rotation is performed to gate the appropriate token (corresponding to A vs. B) into the output subspace.
abstract: Recent work has identified a set of emergent symbolic mechanisms that support abstract reasoning in large language models, but it remains unclear what factors drive the emergence of these mechanisms. To address this question, we trained neural networks from scratch on abstract sequence tasks, varying both architectural and data distributional factors, and investigated the effects of these factors on the emergence of symbolic mechanisms. Using representational, attentional, and causal mediation analyses, we first confirmed that transformer-based language models trained from scratch on our task developed symbolic mechanisms. We then found that, across multiple axes of data diversity, greater diversity produced stronger symbolic signatures. Surprisingly, the same signatures emerged in modified transformer architectures and even multilayer perceptrons, indicating that architectural inductive biases are not necessary for the development of symbolic mechanisms. We also observed consistent patterns in an entity-attribute binding task. Together, these findings identify data diversity, not architecture, as the primary driver of emergent symbolic computation in neural networks.
